title: Show HN: Muxer – Control cmux terminals from Android
text:
Hey HN! As an avid user of cmux (https://cmux.com/), I wanted a way to control terminal and agent sessions from my Android phone, so I built Muxer. The app talks to a tiny relay over HTTPS, that then talks to cmux through its local socket, and gives you to ability to:

  - Answer agent permission requests, questions and plans from a notification
  - Reply to Claude Code, Codex and Pi chat sessions with text, voice, @ file mentions and photos
  - Receive all cmux notification, with inline replies, bubbles and background delivery.
  - Use a live terminal with sticky modifier keys and local scrollback
  - Share text and links from any app to an agent
  - Organize workspaces
  - Manage cmux Cloud VMs and automations
  - Lock the app with your fingerprint, face or screen lock
Enjoy, and let me know what you think!

title: Re: Liella: A Glibc Reimplementation in Rust...
text:
Disclaimer: The Liella project is entirely LLM generated, and is a collaboration between me and Claude Code.

Hi! (I read all the tips, so I'm typing this in by hand, no LLMs here):

A few weeks ago, I had an idea: what would happen if I took a massive codebase and reimplemented it from first principles? So I sat down with Claude Code, told it to generate specs and never consult glibc source ever again, and see what it generated. 400,000 LOC or so later, and I have something that's nearing ready for release. It currently implements nearly all of glibc, and currently significant effort is being put into making it performant. Most code (especially on the hot paths) is at parity with or significantly faster than glibc (16% or so on average, and some regex or local based code is twice as fast). Some code (particularly on the cold path) is still slower but I'm working on improving that. I'm driving towards a release soon - maybe in a couple of months. I still have to build the dynamic loader. Coreutils currently compiles and runs against it, and that's part of the core test suite.

I did build most of this project in rust, mostly because in this case I thought it was the right tool for the job. Some code on the hot path is implemented in C/assembly, and there's a C ABI that has entry points into the rust code. The goal is to be drop-in compatible with glibc in the vast majority of cases.

I'm looking for people who are interested in taking this further - maybe testing on other platforms, helping to work on performance, starting work on the dynamic loader phase, or just code and documentation cleanup (Claude is not perfect).

This is a 100% LLM generated project, so if that's not your cup of tea, I understand. No hard feelings. But if this sounds like it's something you're interested in helping with, I'd love to hear from you!

Code in URL. This is not a fly by night project - I've invested significant resources into this, and will continue to do so.

You can contact me at liella@koiren.ai if you're interested, or comment here.

Thanks!

title: Re: Challenge Is Gone...
text: Hmm, sometimes I feel like living in a different universe. Since LLMs can solve any technical challenge (like most of you claim here) and help folks explore new fields and revive all sorts of projects, wouldn't be all seeing effect of that everywhere? Wouldn't the bar for software quality go up (and go up significantly)? Wouldn't we see new innovative apps that people are delighted to use and more than happy to pay money for? Yet when I recently challenged some friends of mine to name just ONE major app / service that became materially better (I'd argue even better at all) or a new/innovative widely adopted by masses outside of pure AI world (Claudes and GPTs), they couldn't name any. Meanwhile, I am looking around and see that banking, insurance, search, social media, cloud computing are getting more bloated, unstable, mediocre and in general of lower quality. Where is all the cool software everybody is talking about? Where are the features from your backlogs that you were finally able to burn through? I am just not seeing it in the real world. Something doesn't add up here.

title: Ask HN: Are people aware OpenAI Dots intercept SSL?
text:
I've already cancelled my OpenAI subscription due to all their recent shenanigans. But before my month ends I thought I'd see what this Dot thing is all about.

First thing I did was install Firefox to test out a project of mine (wouldn't work in Chrome). It failed to connect:

> The cloud proxy uses an OpenAI certificate authority that the operating system already trusts, but the fresh Firefox profile doesn’t. The game’s connection verifies successfully against that existing authority.

> May I add that same cloud certificate authority to this isolated Firefox test profile? Certificate validation stays enabled, but Firefox would then trust certificates issued by the cloud proxy.

Wait. What? No. Of course not.

Aren't Dots ostensibly designed for personal use? Accessing your email and the like. With this thing intercepting web traffic, I imagine almost everyone using these things are in violation of all sorts of policies and agreements.
